papers.title: Sustained Activation of a Defensive Behavior-Related Circuit Elicits a distinct Homeostatic Sleep Response
papers.abstract: Animals and humans often forgo sleep in response to other physiological needs. Prolonged wakefulness leads to a compensatory homeostatic sleep response involving enhanced amounts of sleep and electroencephalographic delta (0.5-4 Hz) power, yet how the type of preceding wakefulness and brain activity affects this response is poorly understood. Here we compared the pattern of brain activity and the homeostatic sleep response following sustained wakefulness induced by either gentle handling (GH), a widely used form of sleep deprivation in rodents; or optogenetic stimulation of neurons involved in avoidance/defensive responses, basal forebrain (BF) vesicular glutamatergic transporter type 2 (vGluT2) neurons. Local infusion of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists partially attenuated the wake-inducing effect of vGluT2-stimulation, but not that of GH, suggesting mediation by other non-glutamatergic BF subtypes. These antagonists also tended to produce more NREM sleep and a shorter NREM latency in the recovery period following vGluT2-stimulation. Both manipulations increased high theta (7-9 Hz) during wakefulness, an effect partially blocked by local infusion of the glutamate antagonist cocktail. Enhanced NREM sleep time and NREM delta power in the recovery period were more pronounced following GH than following vGluT2 stimulation. Whole-brain cFos immunohistochemistry revealed stronger neuronal activity in brain regions involved in stress and avoidance/defensive behaviors with vGluT2 stimulation, compared to GH. Our results demonstrate that activation of a brain system involved in defensive behavior (BF vGluT2) elicits a distinct and diminished homeostatic sleep response compared to GH, potentially an evolutionary sleep adaptation which would maintain vigilance in the face of an ongoing threat.

papers.title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models
papers.abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.

papers.title: Clocks and steroids interaction across the life span.
papers.abstract: The circadian system enables organisms to anticipate daily environmental changes and to align physiology and behaviour with the external light-dark cycle. In mammals, this temporal organisation is coordinated by the central pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which synchronises peripheral clocks through humoral and neural signals throughout the body. The circadian clock and steroid hormones are linked through a reciprocal, multi-level regulatory relationship. While the SCN and peripheral clocks shape the temporal pattern of steroid secretion, steroid hormones feed back onto the SCN and peripheral clocks, thereby modifying clock gene expression, phase, amplitude, synchrony, and network coherence. This interaction is dynamic across the lifespan, as both the clock and the steroid environment change during development, reproductive life, and ageing. During prenatal and early postnatal development, maternal glucocorticoids (GCs) and other perinatal steroid signals provide time-dependent cues that may shape the maturation and long-term function of the circadian system. During reproductive life in females, ovarian steroids dynamically remodel clocks within the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis, coordinating reproductive timing with circadian signals from the SCN. In parallel, GCs interact with the reproductive axis and may influence fertility in a time-of-day- and cycle-stage-dependent manner. Disruption of this temporal coordination, for example, by shift work, may impair reproductive and endocrine function. With advancing age, both circadian and endocrine rhythms lose robustness, leading to weakened coordination between the SCN and peripheral clocks, as well as reduced synchrony among cellular clocks within peripheral tissues. These changes contribute to disturbed sleep-wake rhythms, reproductive ageing, and altered stress responsiveness. This review discusses the interaction between steroid hormones and circadian clocks across the life span, highlighting reciprocal regulation as a key mechanism linking temporal organisation to physiology and health.

papers.title: Circadian phase alignment promotes survival under predictive oxidative stress
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that continue to oscillate with a period that approximates 24 h in the absence of cyclic environmental cues. This free-running period (FRP) varies from species to species and can vary within species across latitudinal clines. Because natural environments provide daily cues that reset circadian clocks to exactly 24 h, the importance of the FRP length is unclear. Using the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus we show that the FRP length alters the alignment of a biological process with an environmental reference, known as phase angle of entrainment, across seasonal photoperiods, thereby repositioning stress response programs relative to the external environment. This phase relationship affects the overall fitness of the organism: strains that position stress-response programs to peak at the time at which the stressor peaks outcompete their early- or late-peaking counterparts. Our results suggest that the FRP length is selected for its ability to adjust the phase angle of entrainment across seasonal photoperiods: the wild-type FRP length was uniquely plastic in its ability to adjust stress-response programs to coincide with the stressor in all photoperiod conditions.

papers.title: The Bern Sleep-Wake Registry: A 25-year multimodal resource for data-driven sleep medicine
papers.abstract: Background: Sleep-wake-circadian disorders are prevalent and contribute substantially to morbidity, mortality and reduced quality of life. Evaluation in real-world settings is essential to capture their complexity and association with long-term outcomes. Most sleep-wake registries are restricted to selected populations, lack systematic integration of objective sleep-wake-circadian assessments with the clinical data and provide limited follow-up. To address these limitations, we established the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry based on real-world data from a tertiary University Hospital sleep center. Methods: The registry includes data from patients referred to the multidisciplinary Sleep- Center at Inselspital, University Hospital Bern (funded in 1990), from the year 2000 onwards who underwent at least one objective assessment such as polysomnography, daytime sleep-wake recordings, vigilance tests, and actigraphy. The registry integrates clinical information, questionnaire scores, outputs of objective assessments and raw signal data, and is regularly updated to incorporate new patients and longitudinal follow-up information. Results: As of September 2025, records from over 11000 patients were evaluated (median age: 50 years (interquantile range 36, 61); 65% male). The most common sleep-wake-circadian disorders were sleep-related breathing disorders (67%), insomnia disorders (15%) and central disorders of hypersomnolence (9%). Available assessments included more than 12000 polysomnographies, 2400 multiple sleep latency tests, 2100 maintenance of wakefulness tests, 1800 vigilance tests and 4500 actigraphies. Conclusions: By longitudinally integrating multimodal deep clinical phenotyping with objective assessments and raw physiological signals, the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry provides a foundation for investigating disease trajectories, identifying novel biomarkers and developing data-driven approaches to precise diagnosis, prognosis and individualized treatment.

papers.title: Intracranial characterization of gamma in humans in response to auditory gratings
papers.abstract: Activity in the gamma frequency range (>30Hz) serves as a neural hallmark of stimulus encoding across multiple sensory modalities. Based on its distinct properties, this activity could be classified as broadband or narrowband oscillations. Visual stimuli, such as a grating, induce narrowband oscillations, which have shown promise as diagnostic markers for neurological disorders. However, such tasks are discomforting for the subjects. These can be made subject-friendly by swapping the stimulus for an auditory one; however, most auditory stimuli elicit a broadband activity. In search of an ideal candidate to induce auditory narrowband oscillations, we previously recorded responses to auditory gratings in electroencephalography (EEG) recordings (Gulati & Ray, 2024) using a passive listening paradigm. We observed a focal sustained broadband increase in high gamma activity (70-150Hz), which was not selective towards any stimulus attributes. Nevertheless, since EEG represents activity of a large population, it remained unclear whether observed activity represented a broadband increase or comprised multiple narrowband rhythms, and whether it was indeed untuned. To elucidate this, we recorded invasively from the regions on and around the superior temporal gyrus, closer to Heschl's gyrus of seven patients undergoing epilepsy resection surgery. Patients were either under anesthesia or fully awake while we presented auditory gratings through loudspeakers. We found a transient increase in broadband gamma activity (30-100Hz) followed by a sustained suppression of beta rhythm (14-28Hz). This broadband gamma was selective for slower spectro-temporal modulations. Our result compares the responses obtained across different recording scales and corroborates that auditory gratings produce broadband but not narrowband gamma activity.

papers.title: EEG Pathology Detection via Clinical Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.abstract: Deep learning models for electroencephalography (EEG) pathology detection achieve competitive accuracy but offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce concept bottleneck models (CBMs) for EEG pathology detection which use clinical EEG biomarkers computed analytically from the signal as a bottleneck to be used for prediction. Those concepts include band power, spectral ratios, alpha peak frequency and amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry and phase locking values. With the backbone based on shallow convolutional neural network (CNN), we compare a black box baseline with two variants of CBMs. The hybrid variant is a classifier receives a residual projection of the backbone features. The pure variant is a CBM where the classifier receives only the predicted concepts. Models are evaluated on abnormality detection and dementia classification followed by concept prediction quality and leakage analysis. Both CBMs approach the baseline on TUAB (82.7-82.9% vs 83.6%) and are 2-5 percentage points lower on CAUEEG (57.9-60.5% vs 62.7%). The pure CBM exhibits concept fidelity concern where the predicted concepts deviate from their ground truth values. Replacing them with their true values causes severe cost on accuracy by 26 and 22 points on TUAB and CAUEEG. The concept fidelity concern is mitigated by increasing the weight of the concept loss to match the ground truth concepts. the mitigation comes with small accuracy cost on TUAB but a relatively larger cost on CAUEEG. The code of the experiments and full logs are available at https://www.github.com/mhmdrdwn/cbm.

papers.title: How aging reshapes implicit learning: behavioral and oscillatory evidence from an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm.
papers.abstract: Most of everyday memory formation occurs without deliberate intent, yet the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding and their reorganization with age remain poorly understood. The present study investigated age-related changes in implicit learning using an EEG-adapted Fast Mapping paradigm (the Disjunctive Inference Implicit Learning Test, DIILT) in 31 younger and 35 older adults, paired with a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and a one-month delayed recognition measure. Behaviorally, younger adults rapidly acquired novel implicit associations across the learning phase, whereas older adults showed persistent reliance on familiar items and limited improvement for novel associations. Critically, both groups successfully retained novel associations after one month, with implicitly learned associations showing greater long-term stability than explicitly encoded ones regardless of age. At the neural level, younger adults exhibited early posterior theta engagement for novel compared to familiar items, which disappeared by the end of learning, consistent with novelty-driven associative encoding. Older adults showed no such theta modulation for novel items, pointing to reorganization of the neural mechanisms supporting implicit encoding. Theta dynamics predicted immediate recognition in younger adults but not in older adults who rather showed theta association with processing speed, suggesting an age-related shift from memory-specific binding to domain-general cognitive resource allocation, consistent with neural maintenance frameworks of cognitive aging. These findings demonstrate that implicit encoding produces durable memory traces across the lifespan but relies on reorganized oscillatory dynamics in aging, with implications for understanding how cognitive aging reshapes everyday memory formation.

papers.title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing and Sleep Fragmentation in Relation to Atrial Fibrillation Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most prevalent cardiac arrhythmias worldwide. This study aimed to evaluate the association between sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), primarily assessed using the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), and AF risk, with additional analysis of sleep fragmentation parameters such as wake after sleep onset (WASO) and arousal index (AI). This systematic review and meta-analysis followed Cochrane Handbook recommendations and PRISMA guidelines, with protocol registration in PROSPERO (No. 127490). Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational cohort studies assessing sleep disturbances and AF were included. MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and Scopus were searched from inception to February 2026. Extracted data included study characteristics, demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, and sleep metrics. Outcomes were incident and recurrent AF. A random-effects model was applied. Twenty-one cohort studies (611,898 participants) were included. SDB was associated with increased incident AF risk (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.41-1.97; I 2 = 66.5%), with consistent Bayesian estimates. A dose-response relationship showed a 2% increase in AF risk per unit rise in AHI. For AF recurrence, 11 studies (n = 1810) demonstrated a significant association (RR 1.55, 95% CI 1.40-1.72; I 2 = 0%), supported by Bayesian analysis. Sleep disturbances are significantly associated with both incident and recurrent AF and may represent modifiable risk factors.

papers.title: NREM sleep microarchitecture is associated with internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning in early adolescence
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: Sleep disturbances are common in youth with anxiety disorders, yet most prior work relies on subjective measures and does not capture underlying neural processes. We examined whether alterations in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep oscillations are present in children with anxiety disorders and whether these features relate to internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning. Methods: Children aged 9-13 years with diagnosed anxiety disorders (ANX; n = 17) and typically developing non-psychiatric comparison participants (NC; n = 26) completed overnight polysomnography. Slow oscillations (SO) and slow and fast sleep spindles were characterized using validated automated detection algorithms. Participants also completed a pre-sleep emotional processing task, and parents provided standardized measures of youth mental health. Group differences and dimensional associations between NREM oscillations, internalizing symptoms, and behavioral indices of emotional processing were examined. Results: Sleep architecture did not differ between groups. Slow spindle duration was shorter in the ANX group. Across the full sample, shorter slow spindle duration was associated with greater internalizing symptoms, whereas higher SO density was positively associated with internalizing symptoms. Children in the ANX group exhibited greater facial emotional arousal and more frequent look-away behavior during the emotional processing task. Across participants, greater emotional arousal and look-away behavior were associated with shorter spindle duration during subsequent sleep. Conclusions: Specific features of NREM microarchitecture were associated with individual differences in internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning during early adolescence. These findings highlight the potential relevance of NREM oscillations for understanding developmental links between sleep and youth psychopathology.

papers.title: Neonatal Pain Assessment After Night Shifts in NICU Professionals: A Within-Subject Exploratory Eye-Tracking Study.
papers.abstract: Night-shift work may influence attention and emotion processing, potentially affecting clinical assessment. We investigated whether neonatal pain evaluation and associated visual-attentional and pupillary responses differed between rested and post-night-shift assessments in experienced NICU professionals. In this prospective within-subject study, 20 NICU professionals evaluated 42 standardized video clips of term neonates exposed to nonnoxious, short noxious, or prolonged noxious stimuli. Participants were assessed after at least 1 day off work and within 2 h after completing one or more consecutive night shifts. Pain ratings, eye-tracking metrics, and pupil diameter were compared between conditions. Overall pain ratings did not differ significantly between rested and post-night-shift assessments (3.56 ± 0.69 vs. 3.61 ± 0.72; p = 0.643; Cohen's d = 0.11). Pupillary responses also showed no statistically significant differences. Exploratory eye-tracking analyses suggested reduced visual exploration after night-shift exposure, including fewer visits across several areas of interest and shorter fixation duration on the infant's body. These secondary analyses were unadjusted for multiple comparisons and should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating. No statistically significant differences in neonatal pain ratings or pupillary responses were detected following routine night-shift work, whereas exploratory eye-tracking measures suggested differences in visual-attentional patterns. Given the small, selected sample and exploratory design, these findings do not establish equivalent or preserved performance between conditions. Larger prospective studies incorporating objective sleep measures and clinically relevant outcomes are warranted.

papers.title: Protective role of high-intensity exercise and lactate against sleep deprivation-induced alterations in hippocampal gene expression and spatial learning.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation impairs cognitive function by disrupting hippocampal signaling pathways essential for memory formation. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) and lactate, a metabolic byproduct of exercise, have demonstrated potential benefits for brain plasticity, but their protective roles during sleep deprivation remain poorly understood. This study investigated the effects of six weeks of HIIT and lactate administration on memory-related gene expression and spatial learning in sleep-deprived rats. Forty-two male Wistar rats were divided into six groups: Control, Sleep Deprivation (SD), HIIT, HIIT + SD, Lactate, and Lactate + SD. After interventions, sleep deprivation was induced for 48 h. Spatial learning was assessed via the Morris Water Maze test, and hippocampal gene expression of PKA, LIMK, and cofilin was analyzed. The results showed no significant differences in spatial learning performance across groups; however, sleep deprivation caused significant downregulation of key genes involved in memory signaling. Both HIIT and lactate treatments effectively reversed these molecular impairments, notably increasing LIMK expression. These findings highlight the molecular protective effects of HIIT and lactate against sleep deprivation-induced cognitive dysfunction and suggest their potential as non-pharmacological strategies to preserve memory function under sleep loss conditions.

papers.title: Information avant la lettre: The mathematical constitution of brain waves in early EEG analysis (1929-1932).
papers.abstract: This article examines the epistemological conditions under which the brain's electrophysiological trace was first constituted as a mathematical object of analysis. Rather than treating information as a cultural metaphor externally projected onto the brain, the paper reconstructs how specific tools of signal analysis made the trace into an object that the informational lineage would come to require. Hans Berger's research of 1929-1931 secured the trace as an effect of nervous processes in the brain, but read it as the signal of a single source. The case study is Günther Dietsch's 1932 paper, the first application of Fourier analysis to the EEG signal. The article shows that spectral decomposition did not merely describe the signal but constituted it as a decomposable causal object, resolving a single continuous curve into a discrete set of components, each varying independently of the rest. No improvement of the recording apparatus could achieve this; only the mathematical intervention could. The case is read through the causal-deflationary theory of information in López and Lombardi (2019), according to which a source informs a destination only when a variable of the destination can be manipulated by the source. What 1932 builds is the object of a theory of information needs, not yet the measure that such a theory would later compute on it. That is what avant la lettre means here: mathematics made the trace informational before the theory existed.

papers.title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification
papers.abstract: Background: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. Methods: This study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. Results: Among the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. Conclusions: The proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

papers.title: Human testis-specific TTRP regulates circadian clock as an evolutionarily young natural antisense transcript of PER2.
papers.abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates a variety of physiological and behavioral processes, endowing the ability to adapt to the cycling environment. Here, we report the identification of TTRP, a TDP-43 pseudogene that emerged in higher Hominoidea species ~8.6 Mya. TTRP is a human testis-specific gene that overlaps with the clock gene PER2 and interferes with PER2 transcription. TTRP encodes a protein that interacts with the clock proteins PER2, BMAL1, and CRY2, and promotes PER2 and CRY1 turnover. The expression of gorilla and bonobo TTRP proteins changes the period and amplitude of circadian rhythms in human cells. Knock-in and expression of human TTRP in mouse testes prolong the brood-interval time and increase the ratio of sperm with high motility. These findings highlight the functional importance of TTRP as a regulator of the circadian clock and suggest that the human circadian clock may be undergoing continuous evolution through the recruitment of novel factors.

papers.title: Event-Weighted Desaturation Burden and Cardiovascular Mortality in Sleep Apnoea: Findings from a Large Community-Based Prospective Cohort.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnoea's prognostic value is limited by reliance on the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI), which fails to capture physiological heterogeneity of respiratory events. We developed a composite metric, event-weighted desaturation burden (EWDB), integrating weighted respiratory event load, regularity of consecutive inter-event intervals, and cumulative desaturation area. We evaluated its association with cardiovascular mortality and its incremental prognostic value compared with AHI and established hypoxic metrics. We analysed 4,904 adults from the Sleep Heart Health Study with baseline polysomnography and adjudicated follow-up. EWDB was derived by combining a respiratory weighted index, a distribution factor based on inter-event interval regularity, and event-linked hypoxic burden (HB). The primary outcome was cardiovascular mortality. Over a median follow-up of approximately 11 years, 341 cardiovascular deaths occurred. In fully adjusted multivariable Cox models, higher EWDB was independently associated with cardiovascular mortality. However, AHI and HB associations were attenuated and lost statistical significance after full adjustment. EWDB (per 1-SD increase) remained robustly associated with cardiovascular mortality, whereas AHI did not. Incorporating EWDB into a comprehensive clinical model provided incremental risk stratification. Similar robust associations were observed for fatal coronary heart disease and incident heart failure. EWDB was independently associated with cardiovascular mortality and provided incremental prognostic information beyond established clinical and sleep-related factors in this cohort. By integrating respiratory event intensity, cumulative burden, and inter-event interval regularity, EWDB may better characterize cardiovascular stress related to sleep-disordered breathing.

papers.title: Circadian Timekeeping in the Tropics: Rhythmic Transcriptome and Diurnal Regulatory Networks in Rubroshorea leprosula.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms allow plants to regulate internal processes to align with daily rhythms in the environment. Comparing circadian clocks across environments is essential because latitude-dependent variation in light and temperature imposes distinct selection pressures that shape the evolution and function of circadian timing systems. However, circadian clock studies have largely focused on temperate and subtropical species, leaving transcriptional circadian networks in tropical plants poorly understood. We report the comprehensive circadian transcriptome of Rubroshorea leprosula, a dominant species in tropical rainforests in Southeast Asia. One sapling was sampled every 4 hours over 48-hour period under constant darkness and used for transcriptomic analyses. Only 283 of 20 748 expressed genes (~1.3%) exhibited significant circadian oscillations, with periods strongly concentrated between 23 and 25 hours. Hierarchical clustering revealed 4 temporal clusters with alternate phases of expression and functional specialization. Comparative analysis identified clear orthologs for all major Arabidopsis circadian clock components, with conserved synteny to Parashorea chinensis, a close relative of R leprosula. Time-lagged cross-correlation network reconstruction identified a characteristic circadian topological similarity with Arabidopsis, including coupled morning and evening feedback loops and paralog expansion that maintained overall structure. Peak expression timing of these core clock genes in the tropical tree was largely consistent with that observed in Arabidopsis thaliana. In contrast, Rubroshorea orthologs showed reduced amplitudes and lower coefficients of variation under this single constant darkness, single-individual condition; because dark-induced damping is common across plants, this pattern is consistent with, but does not establish, reduced circadian robustness in R leprosula linked to tropical adaptation. This study lays the molecular foundation for circadian regulation in dipterocarps and offers a system for integrating rhythmic gene expression to ecological function and forest productivity in tropical communities.

papers.title: Time-of-Day Variation in Knee Extensor Strength and Fatigue Is Associated With Circadian Phenotype in Healthy Young Adults.
papers.abstract: Time-of-day variation in neuromuscular performance is well established, but the contribution of circadian phenotype remains unclear. This study examined whether maximal knee-extensor strength and fatigue resistance differ between morning and evening and whether chronotype and actigraphy-derived sleep-timing are associated with diurnal performance variation. Forty-four healthy young adults (21 males, 23 females) completed a randomised-crossover protocol consisting of neuromuscular testing in the morning (0700-0900) and evening (1700-1900). Participants completed 7 days of actigraphy monitoring and the Composite Morningness Questionnaire to characterise behavioural circadian phenotype. Sleep timing was assessed using habitual sleep midpoint (between sleep-onset and wake-time), with night-to-night variability in sleep midpoint used as an index of sleep-timing variability. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC) torque, fatigue index, contractions completed, and time-to-exhaustion were assessed during each trial. Baseline MVIC torque was greater in the evening compared with the morning (2.96 ± 0.80 vs 2.85 ± 0.77 N m kg⁻1; P < .0001), with post-fatigue torque also remaining higher in the evening (2.00 ± 0.60 vs 1.84 ± 0.54 N m kg⁻1; P < .0001). Participants demonstrated a lower fatigue-index (32.57 ± 6.99 vs 35.58 ± 6.26%; P < .0001), completed more contractions (37.95 ± 8.29 vs 35.09 ± 7.58; P < .0001), and exhibited longer time-to-exhaustion (6.36 ± 1.51 vs 5.85 ± 1.26 minutes; P < .0001) during evening testing. Chronotype was strongly associated with the PM-AM difference in MVIC torque (r = -.684, P < .0001), explaining 47% of the variance in diurnal performance responses. Neither habitual sleep midpoint (r = -.029, P = .848) nor night-to-night variability in sleep midpoint (r = -.055, P = .721) was associated with performance differences. No significant sex-related differences were observed. Maximal knee extensor strength and fatigue resistance were enhanced during evening compared with morning testing. The magnitude of this response was strongly associated with behavioural circadian phenotype, but not actigraphy-derived sleep-timing. Findings suggest that chronotype influences time-of-day differences in neuromuscular performance and should be considered when evaluating exercise performance.

papers.title: Effects of morning versus evening high-intensity exercise on electroencephalographic and autonomic responses in middle-aged women.
papers.abstract: The time of day at which exercise is performed influences physiological responses and performance, and thus its health benefits. This study investigated whether electroencephalographic (EEG) and autonomic nervous system responses to morning versus evening exercise differed in middle-aged women. Thirty women aged 50-60 years were randomly assigned to a morning or evening exercise group. Participants were asked to sleep for seven to eight hours before testing. The morning group exercised at 6:00 am and the evening group at 6:00 pm. EEG-derived indices included the theta-to-beta ratio (TBR) and spectral edge frequency at 90% (SEF-90). Photoplethysmography-derived autonomic indices comprised the HRV index and HRV-derived sympathetic-related and parasympathetic-related indices, measured at rest before and immediately after exercise. Data were analyzed using a two-way mixed-design analysis of variance. For significant interactions, simple effects and change-score analyses were performed. TBR and SEF-90 showed significant group × time interactions, with greater changes from pre- to post-exercise in the morning group. TBR increased and SEF-90 decreased following exercise in both groups, with greater changes in the morning group. The HRV index showed only a significant main effect of time. However, HRV-derived sympathetic-related and parasympathetic-related indices demonstrated significant group × time interactions, with greater autonomic responses in the morning group, as measured by change scores. EEG- and HRV-derived neurophysiological response patterns to high-intensity exercise may vary with exercise timing. Morning high-intensity exercise may elicit greater neurophysiological responses than evening exercise, highlighting the importance of exercise timing in training strategies and recovery.

papers.title: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Effects on Pulmonary Hemodynamics and Left Ventricular Function in Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) are strongly linked to pulmonary hypertension and left ventricular abnormalities, driving cardiovascular issues. OHS, with daytime hypercapnia, affects 10%-20% of OSA patients. Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is the first-line therapy, but its cardiac effects are inconsistent. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis adhering to the PRISMA 2020 statement. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 (RCTs) and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS; cohort studies). Continuous outcomes were pooled as mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs using random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood) with Hartung-Knapp adjustment. Eight studies (574 participants; 2 RCTs, 6 cohorts) were included, showing that CPAP significantly reduced pulmonary arterial pressure (MD = -2.32 mmHg, 95% CI: -3.88 to -0.76, p = 0.004) versus controls. Secondary analyses indicated improved left ventricular diastolic function (early-to-late diastolic mitral inflow velocity [E/A] ratio: MD = 0.29, 95% CI: 0.09 to 0.48, p = 0.004). No significant effects on left ventricular mass index (LVMi) (MD = -2.31 percentage points, 95% CI: -6.38 to 1.77, p = 0.27) or left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) (MD = 0.53 percentage points, 95% CI: -1.49 to 2.55, p = 0.61) were found. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness. Funnel plot analysis suggested potential publication bias for pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP)/mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP), E/A ratio, and LVEF, while LVMi showed low bias. In adults with OSA or OHS, CPAP reduces pulmonary arterial pressure and improves LV diastolic function, but it does not significantly alter LVMi or ejection fraction. These findings support CPAP as a key intervention to mitigate pulmonary hemodynamic burden and diastolic dysfunction in this high-risk population, while its potential to reverse structural cardiac remodeling requires further study.

papers.title: When Time Online Tells Us Little: Duration of Social Media Use does not Influence Sleep Disruption or Psychopathology in Adolescents
papers.abstract: Background: Adolescent mental health problems have risen alongside increasing sleep disruption and widespread social media use (SMU). However, the mechanisms linking these factors remain unclear. This study concurrently examined objectively measured sleep and SMU in relation to psychopathology to test whether SMU moderates the sleep-mental health association and to characterize day-to-day bidirectional relations among sleep, affect, mood, and SMU during the school year. Methods: Eighty-five adolescents (ages 12-18) completed 14 days of wrist actigraphy, smartphone-based ecological momentary assessments of mood and affect, and objective SMU duration tracking. Cross-sectional models tested whether SMU moderated associations between sleep and psychopathology, and multilevel daily models examined within-person lagged associations among sleep, SMU, and affect, controlling for age and sex. False discovery rate correction was applied. Results: Shorter average sleep duration and greater variability in sleep duration between weekdays and weekends were associated with higher psychopathology symptoms, primarily externalizing problems. SMU duration neither moderated nor directly predicted psychopathology or sleep. Within-person analyses showed that longer-than-usual sleep predicted more positive and less negative affect and lower next-day SMU, though these associations did not survive correction for multiple comparisons. Conclusions: Sleep disruption showed consistent associations with adolescent psychopathology, whereas the amount of time spent on social media did not. These findings suggest that duration-based measures of SMU may incompletely capture adolescents digital experiences and highlight the need for more granular, context-sensitive indicators of online behavior in understanding youth mental health.

papers.title: Vascular brain injury modifies the relationship between sleep duration, cognition, and white matter hyperintensity burden in the Alzheimer's disease continuum.
papers.abstract: Self-reported sleep duration is associated with dementia-risk and vascular brain injury markers, including white matter hyperintensities (WMHs), yet how additional cerebrovascular pathology alters these relationships remains unclear. In a deeply phenotyped cohort (735) including healthy and Alzheimer's disease (AD) continuum individuals (subjective and mild cognitive impairment [MCI], dementia [AD], MCI and AD with high vascular burden [+V]), sleep was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Individuals were classified as WMH-only or WMH+ (WMHs with microbleeds, infarcts, or cerebral amyloid angiopathy). Linear models tested interactions between sleep duration, WMH+ status, and diagnostic group on WMH burden and cognition. In MCI+V and AD, WMH+ significantly amplified the association between shorter sleep and greater WMH burden. In AD, longer sleep related to better cognition in WMH+ but worse cognition in WMH-only (exploratory). Additional vascular brain injury modifies how sleep relates to WMH burden and cognition across the AD continuum, highlighting the importance of moving beyond WMHs alone.

papers.title: Brief Trains of Closed-loop TMS Induce Controllable Power in FM-theta Oscillations
papers.abstract: Objective. Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta; 4-8 Hz) oscillations are thought to support cognition. Brief trains of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can probe these oscillations with high temporal precision but have rarely changed theta power. One possible reason is that prior studies ignored the instantaneous phase of the oscillation, which strongly shapes the cortical response to TMS. We tested whether brief TMS trains triggered at specific FM-theta phases in real time directionally modulate post-train FM-theta power. Approach. Six healthy adults received TMS over dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Fz) with concurrent electroencephalography during a whole-report working memory task. A beamformer and real-time phase-estimation pipeline triggered four-pulse 6 Hz trains (110% of resting motor threshold) at FM-theta peaks (0 degrees) or troughs (180 degrees), randomized trial by trial. Post-train spectral power was decomposed into total, induced (non-phase-locked) and evoked (phase-locked) components. Main results. Trough-triggered trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power relative to peak-triggered trains; task performance did not differ. Cluster-based permutation tests showed trough-peak differences in total (4.6-7.1 Hz) and induced (5.0-7.8 Hz) power ~50-440 ms after the train, suggesting amplification of the oscillation . No evoked effect was detected. The total-power effect was robust at the subject level (Cohen's dz = 1.32, p = 0.023). Within-train theta power did not differ between conditions, suggesting a cortical origin. Significance. To our knowledge, this is the first study to lock brief rhythmic TMS trains to the real-time phase of an ongoing oscillation, and to show phase-dependent modulation of FM-theta power after individual trains on timescales relevant to behavior. Open-loop brief-train protocols may have missed such effects by mixing faciliatory and suppressive phases. Phase-locked brief trains offer a precise tool for testing the causal role of oscillations in cognition.

papers.title: The link between inflammation and autonomic dysfunction in alpha-synucleinopathies - narrative review.
papers.abstract: Alpha-synucleinopathies are a group of disorders characterized by the accumulation of the pathological form of alpha-synuclein. This group comprises Parkinson's disease, Parkinson's disease dementia, multiple system atrophy, dementia with Lewy bodies, pure autonomic failure, and idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder. Despite sharing a similar molecular basis, these disorders differ in their clinical presentation. Characteristic manifestations include signs of autonomic failure such as orthostatic hypotension, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, constipation, gastroparesis, urinary incontinence, and erectile dysfunction, among others. These symptoms significantly impair patients' daily functioning and are also negative prognostic factors. Currently, research is investigating the link between inflammation and dysautonomic symptoms. Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, and IFN-α, have been found to accompany these symptoms. Notably, in other diseases characterized by chronic inflammation, autonomic dysfunction is also common. In two human studies of dysautonomic symptoms in other conditions, intravenous immunoglobulin therapy was shown to improve these symptoms. Animal studies have shown that other immunomodulatory agents reduce symptom severity. Modulation of inflammation, dietary modification, the use of probiotics and prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation are potential therapeutic approaches for these diseases. These approaches offer hope for improving the quality of life of patients with alpha-synucleinopathies. Further research in this area is needed.

papers.title: Rethinking Obstructive Sleep Apnea Care in Obesity: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure, Incretin-Based Therapy, or Both?
papers.abstract: Obesity is a primary driver of obstructive sleep apnea and contributes substantially to its associated cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Although continuous positive airway pressure remains the standard treatment, its efficacy is often limited by suboptimal patient adherence and its impact on cardiovascular outcomes has yet to be consistently established in major clinical trials. Treatments aimed at the underlying problem, excess adiposity, are therefore needed. Weight loss, whether achieved through lifestyle interventions or bariatric surgery is well-known to improve obstructive sleep apnea. The recent introduction of highly effective weight loss medications, most notably incretin-based agents, now offers a pharmacological approach to accomplish the same result. Recent randomized controlled trials in patients with obesity demonstrated that these medications significantly decrease the apnea-hypopnea index and enhance oxygen saturation, with a significant proportion of disease remission. In light of these findings, we propose a therapeutic algorithm stratifying treatment according to symptoms and body mass index. For asymptomatic patients with obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, we suggest incretin-based therapy as a first-line option to concurrently address excessive weight and obstructive sleep apnea. Conversely, in individuals with impaired sleep-related quality of life combining continuous positive airway pressure and incretin therapy may be more appropriate, pairing immediate symptom control with longer-term weight loss. This integrated strategy, prioritizing weight management alongside symptom relief, may offer a comprehensive approach to treat obesity-related obstructive sleep apnea and decrease its associated cardiovascular risks.

papers.title: From Mechanistic Evidence to Clinical Translation: A Narrative Review of Chinese Herbal Medicine for Insomnia.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is one of the most common sleep disorders and a major public health problem worldwide. Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) is widely used as a complementary and alternative approach for chronic insomnia. Clinical studies have reported preliminary evidence of benefit for Chinese herbal formulas, whereas mechanistic research has examined single herbs, extracts, active constituents, and compound formulas using multi-omics analysis, network pharmacology, molecular prediction, and experimental validation. However, clinical studies are typically small and of inconsistent methodological quality, with limited long-term follow-up, while mechanistic evidence remains fragmented and lacks systematic integration and translational validation. These limitations restrict the development of CHM interventions from experimental evidence to clinically testable interventions for insomnia. This narrative review evaluates existing research across five translational dimensions, namely chemical characterization and preparation quality, exposure and pharmacodynamic evidence, mechanism and target validation, sleep-related clinical endpoints, and safety. It aims to clarify the current state of research on CHM interventions for insomnia and to identify key limitations and priorities for future research. Most available evidence comes from preclinical studies, which suggest that CHM may influence sleep-related processes through γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and serotonergic signaling, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis-autophagy balance, and the brain-gut-microbiota axis. Much of this evidence reflects changes in biochemical markers or pathway activity, while only a few studies directly test target function. Clinical studies provide preliminary evidence of short-term improvements in subjective sleep outcomes. However, clinical translation remains limited by insufficient evidence for objective sleep improvement and long-term efficacy and safety. Future work should carry a few well-characterized interventions through the full evidence chain, prioritizing standardized preparations, exposure and pharmacodynamic assessment, objective sleep endpoints, long-term follow-up, and safety.

papers.title: Occupational stress and mental health of police officers in Nigeria.
papers.abstract: BackgroundPolice officers are exposed to occupational stressors; however, little attention is given to the effect of the stressors on their mental health and well-being in many low- and middle-income countries.ObjectiveTo determine the prevalence of operational and organizational stressors and the association with psychological well-being and common mental disorders among police officers in Nigeria.MethodsA total of 1224 randomly selected police officers in four states of Nigeria were interviewed. Validated instruments, including the perceived stress scale, police stress questionnaire (operational (PSQ-Op)/ organizational (PSQ-Org), 12-item general health questionnaire (GHQ-12), 9-item patient health questionnaire (PHQ-9), 7-item generalized anxiety disorder scale (GAD-7), Pittsburgh sleep quality index (PSQI), and the alcohol, smoking, and substance involvement questionnaire (ASSIST), were administered. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Student t-test, ANOVA, and linear regression.ResultsThe overall mean scores on the PSQ-Op (4.24 (sd-1.25)) and PSQ-Org (4.20 (sd-1.25)) were indicative of severe stress. The rates of psychological distress were 22.9%, sleep disturbance- 51.8%, depression- 4.7%, and anxiety- 3.1%. Police occupational stress was associated with service location, perceived stress, psychological distress, sleep disturbance, depression, and anxiety symptoms in bivariate analysis. Perceived stress, sleep disturbance and service location remained significantly related to operational and organizational stress in multivariate analysis while PHQ-9 score was associated with PSQ-Op but not to PSQ-Org.ConclusionPolice officers in Nigeria experience an excessive amount of stress related to their work, and this stress is associated with poor mental and emotional health and is determined by the service location.

papers.title: Cardiac fibrosis and heart failure: Metabolic stress, circadian dysregulation, and extracellular matrix remodeling.
papers.abstract: Diabetes is a major risk factor for heart failure and drives a distinct cardiomyopathic phenotype characterized by oxidative stress, metabolic inflexibility, mitochondrial dysfunction, and progressive myocardial remodeling. Central to this process is cardiac fibrosis, marked by excessive extracellular matrix deposition, increased myocardial stiffness, and impaired mechanotransduction. Emerging evidence identifies circadian rhythm disruption as an under recognized modifier of diabetic cardiac fibrosis. The circadian clock regulates daily oscillations in myocardial metabolism, redox balance, inflammatory signaling, and extracellular matrix turnover, thereby maintaining cardiac homeostasis. However, modern urbanization has introduced chronic exposure to artificial light at night, particularly blue light from digital devices, which suppresses melatonin and desynchronizes central and peripheral clocks. In diabetes, loss of circadian regulation amplifies TGF-β signaling, Rho-A/ROCK-mediated mechanotransduction, oxidative stress, and myofibroblast transformation. Understanding how circadian misalignment accelerates profibrotic remodeling may reveal novel chronotherapeutic strategies to reduce cardiac fibrosis and heart failure risk.

papers.title: Reclaiming agency: how women build mood, confidence and social connections during perimenopause.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to understand women's lived experiences of perimenopause, with reference to brain fog, mood, confidence and social connectedness, and identify opportunities to promote well-being. A qualitative, exploratory study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with 30 midlife women in Australia from culturally diverse backgrounds. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants described perimenopause as a recurring disruption-stabilization cycle rather than a linear decline. Destabilization was often triggered by sleep loss, cumulative life load and symptom variability, shaping appraisals of mood and confidence. Brain fog was experienced as cognitive disruption accompanied by fatigue and self-doubt, commonly worsened by stress, poor sleep and diet. Participants actively engineered stability using individualized, multi-component strategies, including pacing and withdrawal, sleep optimization, physical activity and well-being practices, organizational and compensatory tools, acceptance and reframing, dietary adjustments, leisure and cognitive stimulation, and social support. Social connectedness was recalibrated, with shifts in engagement, mixed experiences of support versus misunderstanding and a strong preference for validating spaces and relationships. Perimenopause was experienced as dynamic yet manageable through structured self-management and supportive contexts. Findings support holistic, multimodal care that integrates symptom management with sleep, behavioral, cognitive and social interventions.

papers.title: Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation in pediatric epileptic syndromes: mechanisms, limitations, and future research horizons.
papers.abstract: Drug-resistant epilepsy affects approximately 20 to 30% of children with epilepsy, with particularly devastating outcomes in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs). Cathodal transcranial direct current stimulation (c-tDCS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulation approach warranting systematic evaluation. Recent meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials demonstrate significant reductions in seizure frequency following c-tDCS compared with sham stimulation, corresponding to roughly 3 to 4 fewer seizures per month or a proportional reduction of about 45% at 4 weeks. Evidence supports efficacy in focal epilepsies and selected syndromes, including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and early-onset epileptic encephalopathies. Standard protocols employ 1 to 2 mA cathodal stimulation for 20 minutes over 5 to 10 consecutive sessions. High-definition tDCS configurations allow more focal current delivery. However, significant inter-individual variability exists, and the relationship between interictal epileptiform discharge suppression and clinical seizure outcomes remains inconsistent. Computational modeling demonstrates substantially higher cortical electric field strengths in children than in adults at equivalent current intensities, raising important dosing considerations. Safety data from over 600 pediatric sessions indicate favorable tolerability with no serious adverse events, although seizure exacerbation has been reported in a minority of participants in open-label studies. Cathodal tDCS represents a safe, tolerable, and potentially effective adjunct to unchanged antiseizure medication regimens in children with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and should presently be regarded as investigational. Selection criteria, optimal stimulation parameters, and syndrome-specific protocols require further refinement. Particular caution is warranted with transcranial alternating current stimulation in generalized epilepsies. Research priorities include closed-loop electroencephalography (EEG)-triggered stimulation systems, biomarker- driven patient selection, age-appropriate dosimetry informed by computational modeling, and adequately powered trials in specific DEE populations including West syndrome, Dravet syndrome, and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation during sleep.

papers.title: Genetic background modulates MafAS64F-mediated islet ageing in male mice.
papers.abstract: In monogenic diabetes, there is increasing recognition that common polygenic factors can modulate diabetes penetrance beyond the causative mutation(s). A naturally occurring mutation in the gene encoding the essential islet-enriched transcription factor MafA (MafAS64F) produces an unusually long-lived variant protein that predisposes male carriers to MODY. Here we investigated how genetic background modulates disease penetrance in MafaS64F/+ male mice. MafaS64F/+ male mice, either on a mixed genetic background (C57BL/6J and SJL/J) or backcrossed to a C57BL/6J background, were assessed for glucose levels, beta cell function and gene signatures associated with cellular ageing. RNA-seq analysis was performed to identify unique differentially expressed genes (DEGS) and pathways in mixed-background or C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mouse islets. These were overlaid on MafA CUT&RUN peaks to identify direct targets that could differentially impact beta cell function in each background. MafaS64F/+ male mice on a mixed background manifested overt diabetes, impaired insulin secretion, accelerated beta cell senescence and dysregulated circadian gene expression, while backcross to C57BL/6J prevented dysglycaemia and maintained insulin secretion in MafaS64F/+ male mice, comparable with control littermates. RNA-seq of C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mouse islets revealed relative normalisation of DEGs associated with cellular ageing and circadian regulation. In addition, islets from C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mice showed unique downregulation of retinoic acid signalling and cell cycle inhibitor p21, the latter of which modulates cellular ageing and diabetes seen in the mixed-background mouse islets. CUT&RUN mapping revealed that MafA directly impacted expression of (at least) retinoic acid receptor-α (encoded by Rara) in islets from C57BL/6J MafaS64F/+ male mice and circadian regulation in islets from mixed-background mice. In sum, these data show that genetic modifiers can impact beta cell regulation of retinoic acid signalling and circadian entrainment to modulate beta cell ageing and disease penetrance in mice modelling MAFA-MODY. Sequencing data were deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (accession no. GSE299343 for bulk RNA-seq and GSE298664 for CUT&RUN analyses).

papers.title: The Association of Window Ventilation Frequency with Depressive Symptoms Among Older Chinese People: Perceived Sleep Duration and Psychological Resilience.
papers.abstract: Little is known about the potential mechanism of window ventilation behavior on depressive symptoms in older people. Associations between window ventilation frequency and depressive symptoms were investigated with modified Poisson regression using the 2018 data of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS), with 11,374 Chinese adults aged 65 years and over. Serial mediation models were applied to investigate if self-reported total sleep duration and psychological resilience mediated the association between window ventilation frequency and depressive symptoms. Window ventilation frequency was negatively associated with depressive symptoms. The mitigating effect of high window ventilation frequency on depressive symptoms had the highest efficacy in spring and the lowest in winter. Window ventilation frequency also had a significant link with depressive symptoms through three significant mediating pathways: the mediating role of self-reported total sleep duration, the mediating role of psychological resilience, and the mediating role of self-reported total sleep duration and psychological resilience, separately. Findings of this study highlighted the mechanism that connects window ventilation behavior to depressive symptoms in older adults.

papers.title: Shift work and hormonal-circadian disruption raise urinary incontinence: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Pelvic floor dysfunction (PFD) is a multifactorial condition that affects a large proportion of women, compromising urogenital support and producing symptoms such as urinary incontinence (UI). The structural and functional integrity of the pelvic floor depends on coordinated interactions among muscular, hormonal, and neuroendocrine systems. Evidence indicates that circadian misalignment, particularly in women exposed to night-shift work, sleep deprivation, and endocrine disruption, can influence pelvic floor physiology through melatonin suppression, cortisol dysregulation, and inflammatory activation. This review intends to synthesize current evidence on the links between circadian rhythm disruption, hormonal imbalance, and PFD, with specific emphasis on occupational shift work as a model of chronic chronobiological stress, highlighting their integrated pathophysiological mechanisms and preventive approaches. We conducted a narrative literature review using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science covering the period from January 2020 to October 2025. Studies investigating the relationship between circadian regulation, hormonal modulation, and pelvic floor function were included. Particular attention was given to research addressing melatonin and cortisol pathways, estrogen modulation, and occupational factors such as night-shift work, sleep deprivation, and physical overload. Eligible study designs included randomized controlled trials, observational studies (cross-sectional and cohort studies), translational and experimental research, and high-quality mechanistic reviews, defined by methodological rigor, comprehensive literature synthesis, and critical appraisal of evidence. Circadian rhythm disruption-characterized by decreased melatonin secretion, altered cortisol levels, and increased oxidative stress-has been associated with inflammation, impaired muscle contractility, and delayed pelvic floor tissue repair. Beyond anatomical alterations, UI is increasingly recognized as a neuroimmunoendocrine disorder in which hormonal dysregulation contributes to tissue instability and loss of urethral support. Women exposed to night-shift work, sleep deprivation, or occupational overload show higher rates of involuntary urine loss, partly mediated by endocrine desynchronization and maladaptive voiding behaviors during chronically misaligned biological rhythms. Preventive measures include supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy, optimization of sleep hygiene, correction of work schedules, and local estrogen therapy when indicated. Chronobiological and immunomodulatory interventions have recently emerged as promising adjunctive strategies. Management of UI should move beyond a purely mechanical perspective toward an integrated model encompassing hormonal, metabolic, and behavioral modulation. Understanding the interactions among circadian rhythms, endocrine control, and pelvic tissue physiology may open innovative avenues for prevention and treatment, promoting precision-based, holistic care in women's health.

papers.title: Sleep trajectories in pregnancy: associations with trauma exposure, PTSD, and postpartum depression.
papers.abstract: Sleep during the perinatal period is often highly disrupted due to maternal biopsychosocial changes that accompany pregnancy. Poor sleep quality is a symptom of PTSD, while insomnia often emerges after a traumatic event and commonly co-occurs with PTSD. Trauma exposure as well as insomnia have been linked to increased risk for postpartum depression (PPD). The current study examined sleep trajectories across pregnancy and into the postpartum period, the impact of trauma exposure and PTSD on these sleep trajectories, and associations between these sleep trajectories and PPD. Participants completed psychiatric diagnostic evaluations for PTSD and other mental health conditions, as well as validated self-ratings of insomnia and depressive symptoms at four time points across pregnancy and at 6 weeks postpartum. Participants were categorized into one of four groups: (a) trauma exposure with PTSD, (b) trauma exposure with another mental health condition, (c) trauma exposure with no mental health conditions, or (d) no reported trauma exposure or current mental health conditions. Longitudinal growth mixture modeling revealed two distinct sleep trajectories across pregnancy: poor sleep (28.5%) and normative sleep (71.5%). Trauma-exposed participants with PTSD or other mental health conditions were more likely to have poor sleep profiles. Participants with poor sleep profiles had significantly higher depressive symptoms. These findings support the need for targeted interventions addressing insomnia in trauma-exposed pregnant women with psychiatric sequelae to improve outcomes during and after pregnancy.

papers.title: The biopsychosocial-spiritual impact upon health information managers from exposure to sensitive information within patient records: A qualitative study.
papers.abstract: Health Information Managers (HIMs) routinely work with patient records containing detailed accounts of illness, trauma and death. While the biopsychosocial-spiritual (BPSS) impacts of trauma exposure have been widely documented among clinicians, little is known about the wellbeing of non-patient-facing health professionals who are repeatedly exposed to sensitive patient information. To explore the BPSS impacts experienced by HIMs following exposure to information contained within patient records. A qualitative study informed by grounded theory methodology was undertaken. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 30 HIMs employed across a range of Victorian healthcare organisations in Australia. Participants were purposively recruited to represent diverse career stages and workplace settings. Interview data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, guided by the BPSS framework. All participants described impacts in at least one BPSS domain, with many reporting experiences across multiple domains. All participants experienced psychological impacts such as empathy, emotional distress, personal resonance, health anxiety, intrusive thoughts, emotional fatigue, desensitisation and positive psychological responses. Three-quarters of respondents experienced spiritual impacts such as existential reflection, moral and ethical appraisal, compassion, helplessness and gratitude. Biological impacts affected over 50% of participants and included somatic (physical) expressions of emotion, sleep disturbances and physical fatigue. Social impacts were least prevalent, affecting only 10% of participants, and included health advocacy within personal networks and social withdrawal. Findings demonstrated that repeated exposure to patient information alone, despite the absence of direct patient contact, was sufficient to influence participants' wellbeing across multiple domains. These findings challenge assumptions that non-patient-facing health professionals, including HIMs, are unaffected by the emotional consequences of patient care and highlight the importance of recognising occupational wellbeing risks associated with indirect exposure to trauma-related material.Implications for health information management practice:Recognition of BPSS impacts should inform workplace wellbeing initiatives and professional support for the HIM workforce. The findings also highlight the need to consider how education and ongoing professional development can better prepare HIMs to recognise and manage the potential wellbeing impacts associated with working with sensitive patient information.

papers.title: From localized to long-range: functional connectivity alterations in mild to moderate chronic low back pain patients.
papers.abstract: Mild pain can influence brain function, yet its central neurobiological mechanisms in chronic low back pain (CLBP) remain insufficiently defined. This study aimed to quantitatively evaluate localized and long-range functional connectivity (FC) alterations in patients with mild to moderate CLBP using static/dynamic regional homogeneity (sReHo/dReHo) and seed-based FC, and to assess their statistical relationships with clinical pain and psychological metrics. A total of 55 mild to moderate CLBP patients and 39 healthy controls (HCs) underwent 3.0 T resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) and clinical assessments, including Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Short-Form of the McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ), Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). sReHo and dReHo (sliding window =50 TRs, step size =5 TRs) maps were computed to identify abnormal localized brain regions. Brain regions showing significant group differences were selected as seeds (6-mm spherical regions of interest, ROIs) for whole-brain FC analysis. Statistical comparisons were corrected using Gaussian random field (GRF) theory (voxel-level P<0.005, cluster-level P<0.05). Partial correlation analyses were used to control for age, sex, education, and head motion (Bonferroni-corrected threshold P<0.007). Compared with HCs, patients exhibited significantly reduced sReHo in the third cerebellar vermis (peak t=-4.253, GRF P<0.05), alongside reduced dReHo in the right parahippocampal gyrus (t=-4.796, GRF P<0.05) and left inferior temporal gyrus (t=-3.935, GRF P<0.05). Seed-based FC analysis revealed decreased connectivity between the third cerebellar vermis and right hippocampus (t=-4.678, GRF P<0.05), and increased connectivity between the left inferior temporal gyrus and left pallidus (t=4.441, GRF P<0.05). Patients showed significantly higher SAS anxiety scores (25.15±5.01 vs. 23.08±2.18, P=0.008). Correlation analyses demonstrated that sReHo in the third cerebellar vermis was negatively correlated with SAS scores (r=-0.384, P=0.005), whereas FC between the left inferior temporal gyrus and left pallidus was positively correlated with SF-MPQ sensory (r=0.381, P=0.006), affective (r=0.386, P=0.005), and total scores (r=0.445, P=0.001). Patients with mild to moderate CLBP exhibit distinct localized and long-range FC alterations within cerebello-hippocampal and cortico-basal ganglia pathways. These neurofunctional changes may contribute to the integration of subjective pain dimensions and comorbid anxiety. Combining static/dynamic ReHo with seed-based FC provides complementary neurobiological insight into how low-intensity chronic pain may affect the central nervous system and highlights the importance of early clinical recognition.

papers.title: An Exploratory Retrospective Comparison of Crisugabalin and Pregabalin Among 12-Week Treatment Completers With Postherpetic Neuralgia.
papers.abstract: Pregabalin (PGB) is commonly used for postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), but its clinical effectiveness may be limited by insufficient pain relief or adverse events (AEs). Crisugabalin (CGB) is a novel α2δ-1 ligand that has demonstrated efficacy in randomized placebo-controlled trials. However, comparative real-world evidence for CGB and PGB remains limited. This single-center retrospective cohort study included patients with PHN who completed at least 12 weeks of CGB or PGB monotherapy between January and June 2025. In October 2025, a single structured telephone interview was conducted to retrospectively assess patients' recalled status at treatment initiation (T0) and at Weeks 1, 4, and 12. Outcomes included the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and the physical and mental component summary scores of the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36). Linear mixed effects models (LMMs) were designated as the primary analyses and adjusted for age, sex, pain location, pre-enrollment pain duration, hypertension, and diabetes. Repeated measures analysis of variance and the LMM analysis based on inverse probability weighting of propensity scores were performed as sensitivity analysis. Safety outcomes were descriptively assessed among treatment completers. A total of 113 patients were included, including 56 in the CGB group and 57 in the PGB group. In the adjusted LMMs, significant treatment-by-time interactions were observed for NRS scores (p < 0.001), PSQI scores (p < 0.001), and SF-36 mental component summary scores (p = 0.003), the extent to which these three scores of the CGB group improved over time may be higher than that of the PGB group. The treatment-by-time interactions were not statistically significant for SF-36 physical component summary scores (p = 0.377). Sensitivity analyses using repeated measures analysis of variance produced concordant findings for NRS, PSQI, and SF-36 mental component scores but not for SF-36 physical component scores. At least one AE was reported by 11 of 56 patients in the CGB group and 18 of 57 patients in the PGB group, but there was no overall significant difference in AEs (p = 0.196). Among patients who completed 12 weeks of treatment, the CGB group was associated with statistical differences to some extent in NRS, PSQI, and SF-36 mental component scores than PGB group, and these degree of improvement over time may be more pronounced. Due to the substantial bias in retrospective studies and the relatively small sample size, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory, merely have reference value, and require more confirmation in prospective controlled studies in the future.

papers.title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists in Multiple Sclerosis: A Topical Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: The glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (RAs) are a relatively new class of drugs that were initially approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to improve glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and, subsequently, weight reduction in patients with obesity. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is commonly associated with comorbidities for which GLP-1RAs are indicated. An increasing prevalence of comorbid chronic diseases has increased the number of people living with MS (pwMS) who are prescribed a GLP-1RA, for indications of obesity, diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, metabolic-associated steatohepatitis, and/or chronic kidney disease. This review addresses the following key considerations: (1) the use of GLP-1RAs for weight loss in pwMS and obesity, including considerations related to drug tolerability and safety; (2) the efficacy of the GLP-1RAs for their approved non-MS indications in pwMS; and (3) the potentially pleiotropic effects of the GLP-1RAs on the MS disease course beyond their approved indications.

papers.title: Perioperative Anesthetic Considerations for Temporal Bone Tumor Resection in Fibroblast Growth Factor 23 (FGF23)-Related Tumor-Induced Osteomalacia: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors (PMTs) are uncommon, predominantly benign neoplasms frequently associated with dysregulated phosphate metabolism through the overproduction of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). Elevated levels of FGF23 lead to phosphate depletion, which may impair tissue oxygen delivery, central respiratory drive, and respiratory muscle function. Systemic manifestations may include osteomalacia and neuromuscular dysfunction, with an increased risk of respiratory and cardiovascular complications. PMTs often present with nonspecific clinical findings and may remain unrecognized during the perioperative period, presenting significant challenges for anesthetic planning and management. We report the case of a 72-year-old male with tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO), a right temporal mass, and multiple comorbidities, including hypertension and obstructive sleep apnea. The patient reported progressive headaches and general weakness. After neurosurgical evaluation, he underwent elective surgical excision under general anesthesia. Intraoperatively, he developed hypotension following induction of anesthesia, requiring vasopressor support with ephedrine boluses and a continuous phenylephrine infusion. The remainder of the procedure was uneventful, and the patient was extubated and transferred to the intensive care unit in stable condition. This case highlights the importance of recognizing potential complications in patients with metabolic abnormalities presenting with PMTs, particularly disturbances in phosphate homeostasis that may have significant anesthetic implications. The use of video laryngoscopy, judicious administration of neuromuscular blocking agents, and an individualized anesthetic strategy facilitated secure airway management, minimized cervical manipulation, and supported an uneventful recovery. Moreover, integrating anesthetic selection with comprehensive perioperative planning is essential to address the metabolic, musculoskeletal, respiratory, and hemodynamic challenges associated with TIO, particularly in patients with significant comorbidities.

papers.title: The Use of Montelukast in Pediatric Asthma and Anti-Inflammatory Effects - Easy Choice or a Balancing Act?
papers.abstract: Montelukast is a selective cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 antagonist with an established, though nuanced, role in the management of asthma and allergic rhinitis. By inhibiting leukotriene-mediated signaling, montelukast targets a pathway involved in bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular permeability, eosinophil recruitment, cytokine release, and airway remodeling. Available evidence indicates that montelukast may reduce several markers of allergic inflammation, including fractional exhaled nitric oxide, peripheral and tissue eosinophilia, eosinophil-derived mediators, adhesion molecules, selected cytokines, and markers related to airway remodeling. These effects are most consistently demonstrated in asthma and allergic rhinitis, while evidence in chronic urticaria, atopic dermatitis, and other inflammatory conditions remains limited or exploratory. Montelukast's once-daily oral administration and age-adjusted pediatric formulations make it a practical option in selected children, particularly when inhaled therapy is difficult or adherence is problematic. However, montelukast should not be regarded as a direct substitute for corticosteroid-based anti-inflammatory therapy. Current evidence and guideline positioning support its use mainly as an add-on controller, or an alternative when more efficacious treatment is contraindicated. The benefit-risk balance is further shaped by concerns regarding neuropsychiatric adverse events, especially in children, although evidence remains heterogeneous. Current data show no increased risk of severe, diagnostically coded neuropsychiatric events, yet milder sleep-related and behavioral symptoms are consistently reported, so that caution and active monitoring remain warranted. Overall, montelukast remains a biologically plausible and clinically useful therapy, but its value depends on appropriate patient selection and realistic expectations of its anti-inflammatory potential.
